name: Centralized Trust
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Putting All Your Trust in One Place, On Purpose
lesson.summary: Centralized trust concentrates verification and authority in a single party, mirroring the client-server model, which buys efficiency and accountability at the cost of a single point of failure.
lesson.body:
The client-server model, the architecture underlying most of the everyday internet, has a simple shape: clients send requests, and a server, or a small cluster controlled by one organization, processes them and sends back answers. Your email provider's servers hold your inbox. A bank's servers hold the authoritative record of your account balance. Centralized trust is what naturally follows from this architecture: when one party controls the authoritative copy of the data and the logic that acts on it, everyone else has to trust that party to keep it honest, available, and unaltered.

The certificate authority system covered in the preceding chapters is a clean example, even though it looks distributed on the surface because there are hundreds of certificate authorities. Within the scope of any single domain's certificate, trust is still centralized in the sense that matters: a small number of entities, ultimately narrowing to whichever root certificate authority anchors the chain, are trusted absolutely, and if that trust is misplaced, there is no independent recourse baked into the protocol itself, only external remedies like removing the certificate authority from trust stores after the fact.

Centralized trust has real, defensible advantages, and it would be a mistake for a skeptical reader to treat it as simply worse. A single authoritative party can move fast, since there is no need to coordinate agreement across independent participants before acting. Accountability is clear: when something goes wrong, there is one identifiable party responsible, one entity that can be regulated, audited, sued, or held to a service agreement. Efficiency is generally higher too, since a centralized system does not need to replicate data or reach consensus across many independent nodes, an overhead that becomes significant in the decentralized systems discussed next.

The cost is equally real. A centralized system has a single point of failure in both the technical sense and the trust sense. If the server goes down, clients cannot function. If the party running the server behaves dishonestly, whether through negligence, insider misuse, or coercion by an outside power, clients have no independent way to detect or prevent it from within the system itself, only after the fact remedies from outside it, much like a compromised certificate authority whose fraudulent certificates look perfectly valid until an outside monitoring mechanism catches them. Every client is also making the same bet on the same party at once, so a single failure affects everyone simultaneously rather than being contained.

Recognizing centralized trust for what it is, an explicit and often reasonable choice to concentrate authority in exchange for speed and accountability, sets up the comparison this book keeps returning to: decentralized trust does not remove the need to trust anything, it changes the shape of what is being trusted, spreading the bet across many parties instead of placing it all on one.
